sweep_summary: Western Cham (west2650) is in the catalog as fixed word-final (iambic) stress, deciding source Ueki 2011 with Friberg & Hor 1977 as supporting primary. the list of works with stress in the title held exactly one stress/prosody-titled item, Ueki 2011, which was already held by the project from the 2026-09-12 ingest (open ScholarSpace bitstream, clean text; I re-opened it at every catalog locator (p.51 sec. 3.7.1, p.118 sec. 6.2.1, pp.135-136 sec. 6.5, p.138, p.163): the quotations are verbatim and the source states the categorical rule ('always occurring on the final syllable'; 'fixed stress on the main, or final, syllable') with acoustic backing, so the item CONFIRMS the catalog's classification; nothing supersedes it. The ScholarSpace landing page (handle 10125/101778) was opened on 2026-09-17 and shows the bitstream as openly downloadable. Copies of Ueki 2011 (PDF + text) and Friberg & Hor 1977 (PDF + scanned text) were placed under and listed in there. The directory already contained, from an earlier check pass, Headley 1991 (Kompong Thom Cham phonology, scanned) and JSEALS 2 (Brunelle 2009); I read Headley's stress passages (final primary stress, secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllables, p.115), which refine the catalog's the secondary-stress rule wording without changing the classification, and Brunelle 2009 only mentions 'sesquisyllabic words with a final stressed syllable' in passing (p.8). only direct download of known URLs was possible. Nothing remains to acquire for this language (priority none across the board).

new_statements.quote: [p.163] WC does not have lexical stress; rather, WC word stress is predictable, always occurring on the final syllable. WC disyllabic words fit into the template of the foot with a weak-strong sequence of syllables. Monosyllables are feet by themselves. [pp.135-136] In each case, Syllable 2 – the main syllable – had a significantly greater value compared to that of Syllable 1, or the pre-syllable. Syllable 2 durations were more than twice those of Syllable 1, indicating that WC words are indeed iambic. Pitch excursion and mean syllable intensity values were also significantly greater for main syllables.

new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final stress in all Western Cham words (iambic weak-strong foot for disyllables, monosyllables as feet), stated categorically at the lexical level and backed by the author's own six-speaker acoustic study (duration >2x, plus greater pitch excursion and intensity on the final syllable). This is the same source and the same passages the catalog already relies on; it confirms the 'fixed' final-stress coding (the rule as stated final stress, domain word). No newer or more authoritative first-hand statement surfaced.

sources.citation: Headley, Robert K. 1991. The phonology of Kompong Thom Cham. In J.H.C.S. Davidson (ed.), Austroasiatic languages: Essays in honour of H. L. Shorto, 105-122. London: SOAS. (Not in the target list; already downloaded into this our files by an earlier reading, see; Kompong Thom is a Cambodian, i.e. Western Cham, variety)
sources.quote: pp.105-106: native word templates mark primary stress (') on the final syllable, e.g. CVCV /pato/ [pa'to:] 'teach', CVCVF /kanon/ [ko'no:n] 'be angry'; polysyllables ''CVCV'CVF with '' = secondary stress on the first syllable, e.g. /panatan/ [''pana'tan] 'animal'. p.115: 'The third syllable receives the main stress while the first receives secondary stress.' (/marasa/ 'maybe', /masatah/ 'from a distance'). Also p.116-area: /a/ in unstressed presyllables reduced.
sources.locator: pp.105-106 (sec. 1 'The Word', syllabic templates with stress marks); p.115 (sec. 3, trisyllables)
sources.note: The one Glottolog 'phonology' ref we did not hold; a different Western Cham dialect (Kompong Thom) from Ueki's Kompong Chhnang/Kompong Cham and Friberg & Hor's Chau Doc; it explicitly marks secondary stress on the initial syllable of trisyllables, which sharpens our the secondary-stress rule ('no secondary stress described beyond weak stress').

sources.note: From the Crossref record and Lee 1998's use of it: sets out the Chamic continuum from conservative onset-voicing languages (Northern Roglai, Rade, Jarai) through register languages (Western Cham, Haroi) to incipient/full tone (Phan Rang Cham, Tsat), the trajectory on which Lee places Cat Gia Roglai at the 'register in development' stage; not known to give CGR-specific tone or register data.
